Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Salesperson
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Richard is a 70-year-old married American man who has spent most of his adult life working as a salesperson, a role that once fit the version of himself he recognized easily: sociable, steady under pressure, comfortable striking up conversation with strangers. The assault happened several months ago at a stop he had made during the workday, near a commercial strip he used to visit routinely to see clients. He had gone in expecting an ordinary errand and instead found himself confronted by a man who was visibly intoxicated. What has stayed with Richard is not only the suddenness of the attack, but the sensory immediacy of it: the sharp smell of alcohol on the man’s breath as he came close, the shock of seeing his face at arm’s length, and the disbelief that things had turned dangerous so quickly. In Richard’s mind, the scene remains tied to that place and to the offender’s appearance in a way that still feels alarmingly immediate.

In the days afterward, Richard told himself he should be able to put it aside. He tried to carry on with work and with life at home with his wife, but unwanted thoughts about the assault kept arriving without warning. They would intrude when he was driving between appointments, when he was setting up for a sales call, or when the day briefly went quiet. He did not experience them as memories he chose to revisit; they came as unwelcome mental returns to the assault, and he would tense as soon as he noticed them beginning. If he caught sight of someone who resembled the offender, even only in passing, his attention would lock onto the person before he could stop it. The same thing happened when he encountered the smell of alcohol. Passing a customer who had been drinking at lunch, walking by a bar entrance, or catching stale liquor on someone’s clothes could pull him abruptly back into the sense that the assault was happening again in some essential way.

Because so much of his work depends on moving through the community, these moments began to shape his days. Richard started avoiding the location where the assault occurred, first by taking a different route, then by declining to stop in that area altogether. He told himself there was no good reason to go near it if he could help it. Over weeks and months, this avoidance became part of how he organized his sales territory. Accounts in that part of town were postponed, reassigned when possible, or visited only after prolonged hesitation. The change affected his work rhythm and narrowed the ease with which he had once moved through his job. Places that used to feel neutral now carried the possibility of seeing the offender again, and he remained alert to that possibility whenever he was out.

At home, Richard put equal effort into trying not to think about the assault. When thoughts surfaced, he pushed them away hard, changing the subject in his own mind or getting up to busy himself with something practical. He found that he was also numbing his feelings more generally. His wife noticed he seemed less emotionally present, as though he had gone flat in situations where he would once have shown warmth or irritation or humor. Richard recognized this too, and it unsettled him. He had come to feel that the person he had become was unrecognizable to him. He did not describe himself simply as shaken; he felt altered in a more fundamental way, as though something about the assault had exposed a defect in him. There was, he believed, something wrong with him as a person if he could not return to normal, if a smell or a glimpse of a man on the street could still throw him off balance.

He also circled repeatedly around the question of his own part in what happened. Richard blamed himself for the way he acted during the assault and in the moments leading up to it. In his telling, he should have read the situation differently, said something else, moved sooner, handled himself in another way. These thoughts did not resolve anything for him, but they remained persistent and personal, folded into a broader conviction that the assault said something shameful about him.

By the time he sought help, Richard was still working, but with increasing strain. The practical detours around that part of town, the constant effort to suppress intrusive thoughts, and the emotional distance that had entered his marriage had all become harder to ignore. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic worsening, but the accumulation of these changes and his growing fear that this diminished, guarded version of himself might be permanent. What he wants most is to feel recognizable to himself again; what frightens him most is the possibility that he cannot.
